title: A galaxy full of surprises: the spiral galaxy NGC 3621
caption: The pure-disc galaxy NGC 3621, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
celestial: NGC 3621 · constellation Hydra · about 22 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: NGC 3621 has a flat disc crossed by dark lanes, with spiral arms where young stars form in clusters that show up as blue dots. Its center simply grows brighter, with no true bulge. Background galaxies and a few bright foreground stars from our own Milky Way also appear.
Most spiral galaxies have a central bulge, a compact, rounded crowd of old stars. NGC 3621 is a pure-disc galaxy and lacks one, unlike NGC 6744, for example.

It is also believed to host an active supermassive black hole that is swallowing matter and giving off radiation. That is somewhat unusual, because such active galactic nuclei are mostly found in galaxies with large bulges. This black hole is thought to be fairly light, around 20 000 times the mass of the Sun, and two smaller black holes of a few thousand solar masses are thought to lie near the nucleus. NGC 3621 may have three black holes at its heart.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (6.81 x 6.81 arcminutes) and distance (22 million light years), the frame spans roughly 44,000 × 44,000 light-years. Its light set out about 22 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: The FORS1 instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope recorded NGC 3621 through B, V and I filters. Young star clusters appear as blue dots, but the full color mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: A moderate-sized telescope shows the galaxy, but not the fine detail here, and the I filter records near-infrared light the eye cannot see.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: The galaxy lies in the constellation Hydra (The Sea Snake), about 22 million light-years away, and a moderate-sized telescope can show it. ESO took this picture with the FORS1 instrument on the VLT through B, V and I filters.
alt: A spiral galaxy with dark dust lanes and blue star clusters in its arms, a center that brightens without a bulge, and background galaxies and foreground stars around it.
